blocks.html: Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory condition where tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus. But for many women, the impact extends far beyond pelvic pain. This affects hormones, digestion, bladder function, energy, sleep, intimacy, and overall quality of life.

items.a: Mild discomfort can happen during cycles, but severe pain that disrupts work, sleep, movement, or quality of life should not be dismissed as normal. Endometriosis pain can be intense, persistent, and connected to inflammation, hormonal sensitivity, nervous system sensitization, and tissue involvement beyond the uterus.

items.q: Why did it take so long for someone to take my symptoms seriously?
items.a: Endometriosis is commonly underrecognized because symptoms can overlap with cramps, IBS, bladder issues, pelvic floor dysfunction, hormonal changes, and chronic stress. Many women are told their pain is “normal” for years before receiving a deeper evaluation. That delay is common, but it should not be acceptable.

items.q: Can endometriosis affect more than the reproductive system?
items.a: Yes. Endometriosis can affect digestion, bladder function, sleep, energy, mood, recovery, inflammation, and nervous system sensitivity. It is not only a reproductive condition or a period-pain condition — it can affect the whole body.

items.q: Why do I feel exhausted all the time?
items.a: Fatigue with endometriosis can come from chronic inflammation, pain, poor sleep, heavy bleeding, iron deficiency, nervous system overload, hormone shifts, and the physical stress of managing symptoms over time. It is not “just being tired.”

items.q: Why does pain sometimes continue between cycles?
items.a: Endometriosis can create ongoing inflammation, tissue irritation, pelvic floor tension, and nervous system sensitization. That means pain may continue even when you are not actively bleeding or in the most intense part of your cycle.

items.q: Is surgery the only treatment option?
items.a: No. Surgery may be appropriate for some patients, especially when lesions need to be removed or symptoms are severe. But endometriosis care can also include hormonal support, inflammation management, pain management, nervous system regulation, pelvic floor therapy, nutrition, recovery support, and coordinated care with specialists.

No. RHM does not perform endometriosis surgery. When surgery is appropriate, that should be handled by a qualified gynecologic surgical specialist, often a minimally invasive gynecologic surgeon. RHM’s role is to support the inflammatory, hormonal, metabolic, nervous system, and recovery patterns that may contribute to symptoms — alongside surgical or gynecologic care when needed.

Yes. Endometriosis is hormonally sensitive, especially to estrogen. Hormone patterns can affect inflammation, pain, cycle symptoms, bleeding, mood, fatigue, and symptom flares. That does not mean every patient needs hormone therapy, but hormones should be part of a thoughtful evaluation.

items.q: Why do digestive or bladder symptoms happen with endometriosis?
items.a: Endometriosis can affect tissue near the bowel, bladder, pelvis, and surrounding nerves. Inflammation and nervous system sensitization can also create symptoms that feel like IBS, bloating, bowel pain, urinary urgency, bladder discomfort, or pelvic pressure.

items.q: Will I automatically be prescribed hormones?
items.a: No. Hormones are not automatic. RHM evaluates your symptoms, medical history, goals, risk profile, labs, and current care plan before making recommendations. Some patients may benefit from hormone-related care, while others may need inflammation support, pelvic floor care, pain management, nutrition, recovery work, surgical coordination, or other interventions.
